body:
What is prehistory?

Prehistory refers to the period of the human past for which written records are not available. Knowledge of prehistoric life comes mainly from material remains such as stone tools, animal bones, traces of settlements and rock paintings.

Prehistoric people were capable of communication, cooperation and practical knowledge. The absence of written records does not mean that they lacked spoken language or organised social life.

The earliest part of Indian prehistory is commonly studied through the Stone Age, when stone was an important material for making tools. People also used wood, bone and other natural materials, but stone objects have generally survived better.

The main divisions of the Stone Age

The Stone Age is broadly divided into the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic periods. These names describe major differences in tools and ways of life. They do not represent changes that occurred everywhere on the same date.

Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age

The word Palaeolithic comes from the Greek words palaeo, meaning old, and lithos, meaning stone. It is the earliest and longest phase of the Stone Age.

The introductory NCERT chronology places the Palaeolithic period from approximately 2 million years ago to 12,000 years ago. During this period, people mainly obtained food by hunting wild animals, fishing and gathering naturally available plant products.

The Palaeolithic is divided into 3 successive phases: Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic.

Mesolithic or Middle Stone Age

Mesolithic means Middle Stone Age. It follows the Palaeolithic and precedes the Neolithic in the conventional sequence.

The Mesolithic is especially associated with small stone tools called microliths, which could be attached to wooden or bone handles. Hunting, fishing and gathering continued, while people adapted to changing environments and increasingly varied their food resources.

Neolithic or New Stone Age

The Neolithic is associated with the increasing importance of food production, animal domestication, more settled communities and polished stone tools. These developments occurred gradually and at different times in different regions.

The Neolithic is mentioned here to establish the boundary of the present topic. The main concern is the earlier Palaeolithic and Mesolithic cultures.

Chronological sequence

PeriodBroad chronological positionCharacteristic tools
Lower PalaeolithicEarliest phase; beginning roughly 2 million years ago in the introductory Indian sequenceHandaxes, cleavers and choppers
Middle PalaeolithicAfter Lower Palaeolithic; often placed around 100,000–40,000 years ago in simplified sequencesFlakes, scrapers and points
Upper PalaeolithicLast Palaeolithic phase; often placed around 40,000–12,000 years ago in simplified sequencesBlades, burins and borers
MesolithicBegins around 12,000 years ago in the introductory NCERT sequence; continued considerably later in several regionsMicroliths and composite tools

Chronological boundaries are approximate

The dates above are teaching approximations, not fixed boundaries for every archaeological site. Middle Palaeolithic technology appeared much earlier than 100,000 years ago at some Indian sites, including Attirampakkam. The introductory NCERT sequence describes the Mesolithic as extending from about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago, but Mesolithic ways of life continued for several millennia afterward in parts of India.

For objective questions, distinguish the established order of cultural phases from a claim that all regions changed simultaneously.

Why tools are important for understanding these periods

Stone tools reveal how prehistoric communities cut, scraped, chopped and processed natural materials. Changes in their size and form help distinguish the major cultural phases.

The general sequence shows a growing variety of specialised tools, from large handaxes and cleavers to flakes, blades and microliths. However, newer forms did not immediately replace older ones. Different kinds of tools could continue to be used together.

Prelims focus

  • Palaeolithic means Old Stone Age; Mesolithic means Middle Stone Age.
  • The Palaeolithic is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases, in that order.
  • Lower Palaeolithic is particularly associated with large core tools.
  • Middle Palaeolithic is commonly associated with flake-based tools.
  • Upper Palaeolithic is especially associated with blade tools.
  • Mesolithic cultures are characteristically associated with microliths.
  • Trap: These technological phases do not have identical starting and ending dates throughout India.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 11–19, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, Timeline and Sources of History, pp. 70–73; INFLIBNET, Outlines of Indian History, Pre-historic Cultures in India, sections 3–4, consulted 17 November 2026; Akhilesh and others, Early Middle Palaeolithic Culture in India around 385–172 ka, Nature, 2018, abstract.]

title: Understanding Prehistory and the Chronology of Stone Age Cultures

body:
The earliest major stone-tool tradition

The Lower Palaeolithic represents the earliest phase of the Palaeolithic sequence. In the Indian subcontinent, it is known especially for large stone implements such as handaxes, cleavers and choppers.

Many of these implements belong to the Acheulian tradition, which is particularly associated with carefully shaped handaxes and cleavers. Another early tool tradition used pebbles and cores modified to produce chopping edges.

Stone tools were useful because a shaped cutting edge could perform tasks that were difficult with an unmodified stone, including cutting animal flesh, chopping wood and processing plant material.

Characteristic tools

Handaxe

A handaxe is usually a relatively large stone implement shaped to produce cutting edges. Many handaxes have a pointed or rounded working end and are worked on both faces of the stone.

The term bifacial means that stone has been removed from both major faces of the implement. The resulting tool could serve several purposes, including cutting, chopping and processing animal or plant materials.

Cleaver

A cleaver is characterised by a broad working edge across one end. Unlike the typically pointed form of many handaxes, its distinctive feature is the broad transverse cutting edge.

Cleavers could be used for heavy cutting and chopping activities.

Chopper

A chopper is commonly made from a pebble or other stone piece by removing flakes from part of its edge to create a working surface.

Choppers are often less extensively shaped than typical Acheulian handaxes. Their principal function was chopping or other heavy cutting work.

Core tools and stone materials

A core tool is an implement in which the main stone piece itself is shaped into a usable tool. The material removed from it consists of flakes, some of which may also be useful.

Quartzite was an important raw material for many Indian Palaeolithic tools because it is hard and can be shaped to produce durable cutting edges. Other stones were used according to local availability.

Prehistoric communities frequently occupied landscapes where suitable stone could be obtained near sources of food and water.

Important Lower Palaeolithic sites

Site or regionPresent locationImportant association
PallavaramTamil NaduDiscovery of an early Palaeolithic handaxe in 1863
AttirampakkamTamil NaduAcheulian handaxes and cleavers; evidence of later Palaeolithic traditions
HunsgiKarnatakaEarly Palaeolithic tools and tool-making locations
BhimbetkaMadhya PradeshEarly stone tools and evidence of occupation over several periods
Soan ValleyPresent-day PakistanEarly pebble and flake tool traditions

Pallavaram and Robert Bruce Foote

On 30 May 1863, geologist Robert Bruce Foote recognised a Palaeolithic handaxe at Pallavaram near present-day Chennai.

This discovery is an important landmark in the recognition of prehistoric stone tools in India. Foote is consequently known as the Father of Indian Prehistory.

The year 1863 refers to the modern discovery of the implement, not the date on which prehistoric people manufactured it.

Attirampakkam

Attirampakkam, in the Kortallayar River basin of Tamil Nadu, is an important site for Lower Palaeolithic Acheulian tools. Handaxes and cleavers are prominent among its early implements.

The site also preserves evidence of later technological changes. It therefore illustrates that a single archaeological location can contain remains of more than one Palaeolithic phase.

Hunsgi

Hunsgi, in Karnataka, is known for several early Palaeolithic sites. Some locations contain numerous tools associated with different activities, while others mainly show evidence of tool production.

The NCERT account notes that limestone was locally available and was used to manufacture many tools in the Hunsgi area.

What Lower Palaeolithic sites reveal

Lower Palaeolithic remains demonstrate that early communities selected suitable stone, manufactured useful implements and repeatedly occupied locations where resources were available.

The widespread distribution of such sites across river valleys and other landscapes indicates adaptation to different environments. It does not imply that every group followed an identical daily routine or used exactly the same tools.

Prelims focus

  • Handaxe, cleaver and chopper are important Lower Palaeolithic tool types.
  • Acheulian technology is especially associated with handaxes and cleavers.
  • A bifacial implement has been worked on both major faces.
  • Robert Bruce Foote discovered a Palaeolithic handaxe at Pallavaram in 1863.
  • Attirampakkam is in Tamil Nadu; Hunsgi is in Karnataka.
  • Trap: The broad cutting edge of a cleaver distinguishes it from the commonly pointed form of a handaxe.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 12–19; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Lower Palaeolithic Culture, sections on tool traditions, sites and explorations, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Outlines of Indian History, Pre-historic Cultures in India, section 3.1; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, account of early stone tools, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Handaxe with two worked faces and a pointed end, cleaver with a broad end edge, and chopper with flakes removed from a pebble edge.
pictures.caption: Recognising the main Lower Palaeolithic stone-tool forms.

title: Lower Palaeolithic Culture: Large Stone Tools and Early Sites

body:
How tools changed after the Lower Palaeolithic

During the later Palaeolithic phases, people increasingly manufactured smaller and more specialised tools. The important distinction is between tools made by shaping a large stone core and tools made from flakes or blades removed from a core.

This development did not occur suddenly or uniformly. Large tools, smaller flakes and blades could coexist within a region.

Middle Palaeolithic culture

The Middle Palaeolithic follows the Lower Palaeolithic in the conventional cultural sequence. It is particularly associated with flake-based stone industries.

A flake is a piece of stone detached from a larger stone or core. Its sharp edges may be used directly, or the flake may be shaped further into a particular implement.

Important Middle Palaeolithic tools

  • Scrapers: tools with working edges useful for scraping hides, wood or other materials.
  • Points: tools with a pointed working end that could be used for piercing or attached to a shaft.
  • Retouched flakes: flakes whose edges were further modified to improve their working shape.

The increased importance of flake tools distinguishes the Middle Palaeolithic from the handaxe-dominated Acheulian tradition. However, some large tools continued to be used.

Stone materials

Quartzite remained important in several regions. Finer-grained stones such as chert and other siliceous rocks were also used to make relatively small cutting tools.

Important Middle Palaeolithic locations

Evidence of Middle Palaeolithic cultures occurs at Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu and several sites in the river valleys and plateau regions of India.

The Orsang region of Gujarat is also associated with Middle Palaeolithic stone-tool evidence.

Upper Palaeolithic culture

The Upper Palaeolithic is the final major phase of the Palaeolithic sequence. It is especially associated with the increased importance of blades and specialised tools.

A blade is a relatively long, narrow piece of stone with approximately parallel sides. Unlike a typical broad flake, a blade provides a comparatively long cutting edge in relation to its width.

Important Upper Palaeolithic tools

  • Blades: long and relatively narrow stone pieces suitable for cutting and further modification.
  • Burins: tools with a narrow, chisel-like working edge, useful for engraving or working hard materials.
  • Borers: pointed implements used for piercing or making holes.
  • Scrapers and other modified blades: tools designed for different cutting and scraping activities.

Important Upper Palaeolithic sites and finds

Bhimbetka

Bhimbetka contains evidence of several Palaeolithic phases. The Upper Palaeolithic assemblage includes blade-related tools such as blades, borers and burins.

Some of the earliest phases of prehistoric painting in the NCERT art-history classification are also assigned to the Upper Palaeolithic.

Patne

Patne in Maharashtra is an important Palaeolithic site. Finds of ostrich eggshells, including pieces bearing engraved designs and examples used for beads, demonstrate the presence of ostriches and the use of eggshell material by prehistoric communities.

These objects also indicate activities beyond the production of ordinary cutting tools.

Kurnool region

The caves of the Kurnool region in present-day Andhra Pradesh have yielded evidence relevant to Palaeolithic occupations. The region is associated with stone tools and, at some cave sites, bone implements.

The main technological distinction

For prelims preparation, the most useful sequence is:

  • Lower Palaeolithic: prominence of large core tools, especially handaxes and cleavers.
  • Middle Palaeolithic: increased importance of flakes, scrapers and points.
  • Upper Palaeolithic: increased importance of blades, burins and borers.

This is a comparison of characteristic technologies, not a claim that any tool type existed exclusively in one period. In particular, blades and small stone tools did not suddenly appear for the first time with the Mesolithic.

Prelims focus

  • Middle Palaeolithic cultures are commonly identified by flake-based tools.
  • Scrapers and points are important Middle Palaeolithic tool forms.
  • Upper Palaeolithic cultures are particularly associated with blades, burins and borers.
  • Patne in Maharashtra has yielded Palaeolithic ostrich eggshell remains, including decorated pieces and beads.
  • Bhimbetka contains evidence from more than one Palaeolithic phase.
  • Trap: Blades are characteristic of the Upper Palaeolithic, whereas small composite microlithic tools are especially characteristic of the Mesolithic. Neither association is absolutely exclusive.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 13–19; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Prehistoric Rock Paintings, pp. 1–4; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, description of Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tools, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Outlines of Indian History, Pre-historic Cultures in India, sections 3.2–3.3, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The broad technological sequence from large core tools to flakes and blades.

title: Middle and Upper Palaeolithic Cultures: The Development of Flake and Blade Tools
